title: Army Weekly Briefing
description: Army leadership, force design, modernization, contracts and the signal and network enterprise.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 9–18. New: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 17 that the White House nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the acting chief, to be Army chief of staff, and Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans to be vice chief. Army.mil reported the same day that Brig. Gen. Marne L. Sutten assumed command of CECOM and Aberdeen Proving Ground on Nov. 16. Federal News Network reported that Army Test and Education Command is booking commercial firms onto six ranges, and that service test officials met at Aberdeen in September. No new NETCOM release and no new Army enterprise agreement were found in Army CIO reporting, ESI, war.gov, Federal News Network, Breaking Defense, DefenseScoop, Nextgov, GovConWire, or vendor newsrooms. The Week Ahead subsection is empty.

items.headline: White House nominates Gen. LaNeve to be Army chief of staff
items.summary: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 17 that the White House formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be the Army's chief of staff, the job he has held in an acting capacity since Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April. Stars and Stripes said the Senate received the nomination Monday and referred it to the Senate Armed Services Committee, and that the White House the same day nominated Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans, director of the Army staff, to be vice chief. Breaking Defense reported that LaNeve said he has served 36 years, currently as vice chief, and that he is honored by the president's nomination. Stars and Stripes said it was not clear whether the Senate would act before a new Democratic majority is sworn in on Jan. 3, and that the White House has not nominated a permanent replacement for former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.

items.headline: Sutten assumes command of CECOM and Aberdeen Proving Ground
items.summary: Army.mil reported Nov. 17 that Brig. Gen. Marne L. Sutten assumed command of the Communications-Electronics Command and the duties of Aberdeen Proving Ground senior commander at a ceremony on Nov. 16. The article said she leads a 9,000-person global command and is senior commander of a 28,000-person installation, and that she is the Army's command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and medical materiel integrator. Lt. Gen. Gavin A. Lawrence, deputy commanding general and acting commander of Army Materiel Command, presided and said Sutten most recently directed network command, control, cyber communications systems integration on the G-6. Sutten said she is the 19th commander of CECOM.

items.headline: President nominates DEVCOM's Aberdeen commander and 35 other Army brigadiers
items.summary: The Department of War said Nov. 16 that Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the president has nominated 36 Army brigadier generals for appointment to major general. The list includes Brig. Gen. Robert G. Born, commanding general of Combat Capabilities Development Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, and Brig. Gen. Marne L. Sutten, who previously served as director of network command, control, cyber communications systems integration in the Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff, G-6. The release announces nominations, not Senate confirmations, and it does not say Sutten has assumed command of CECOM.

items.headline: CNBC: British police arrest a U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia
items.summary: CNBC reported Nov. 11 that London's Metropolitan Police said a 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier was arrested near Gloucester, England, on Tuesday on suspicion of spying for Russia, and that he is being held under the U.K. National Security Act. CNBC said a senior NATO official confirmed the soldier was assigned to the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, and that police worked with U.S. military authorities and the FBI. FBI Director Kash Patel said the allegations were of the utmost concern, and Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said the alleged conduct is a reminder that insider threats are real. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Moscow had absolutely nothing to do with the case.

items.headline: Army Test and Education Command is booking commercial firms onto six ranges
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Nov. 17 that Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon, commanding general of Army Test and Education Command, said more than 120 companies have tested prototypes or are in the pipeline across six Army ranges since an initiative launched in August. The Army said 15 companies have completed tests on drones, counter-drone systems, missile interceptors, and long-range strike technologies, 14 are ready to proceed, and 93 are in the works, at Dugway Proving Ground, Yuma Proving Ground, Camp Grayling, Camp Atterbury and Muscatatuck, and a U.S.-run range in Morocco. Gaydon said the service is trying to bring firms in within 30 days of a request and now averages 33 days. Federal News Network said test officials from the other services met at Aberdeen Proving Ground in September, and that Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro said last month the Air Force is working with the Army on whether it could open its own ranges to commercial companies.

items.headline: Army Contracting Command opens a Manufacturing Rodeo for 400 one-way-attack drones
items.summary: DRONELIFE reported Nov. 16 that a Nov. 13 Army Contracting Command solicitation outlines a small-uncrewed-aircraft Manufacturing Rodeo pairing commercial manufacturers with the Army's organic industrial base. DRONELIFE said the effort covers Group 1 first-person-view one-way-attack and loitering-strike drones, with an initial batch of 400 flight-ready aircraft and 20 ground control stations at a maximum unit price of $3,000, and that the Army would supply batteries, motors, frames, and other specified equipment. The aircraft would compete at Drone Dominance Gauntlet III in March 2027, and successful participants could qualify for follow-on production of up to 10,000 aircraft at Army depots. DRONELIFE said a virtual industry briefing was scheduled for Nov. 16 and that the solicitation lists Nov. 20 as the overall response date, with an earlier deadline for initial solution briefs.

items.headline: Grafenwoehr test fires containerized drone swarms and robotic Javelin launchers
items.summary: Stars and Stripes reported Nov. 13 that soldiers at Grafenwoehr Training Area on Thursday attacked targets with weapons stored in shipping containers, drones, and unmanned vehicles. The demonstration began with an unmanned ground vehicle carrying two Javelin launchers, and another unmanned ground vehicle then fired a swarm of 18 drones from a pre-positioned container. Col. Michael Weisman, a senior spokesman for the Army in Europe, said in a statement Friday that the systems are part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative. Alex Tomosieski of the Combat Capabilities Development Command said the Army wants to store drones and unmanned ground vehicles in containers under a program called the Remote Rapid Response Contingency Team.

items.headline: Army Materiel Command says small attack drones will be replaced, not stockpiled
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 12 that Jon Strzelec, Army Materiel Command's advanced manufacturing lead for small drones, said the Army told his team that small drones will not be stored on shelves and that the service will manufacture to deliver, not to stock. He said a countermeasure can appear within 72 hours in Ukraine, and that building a new drone is cheaper than pulling a circuit card, flashing software, and returning the aircraft to service. He said the Army was receiving 10,000 of the first 30,000 small drones from Drone Dominance Gauntlet 1, and that those aircraft go to units for training and are not sustained after they break. He said Group 2 drones, which he described as 21 to 55 pounds and used for reconnaissance or delivery, are more likely to be kept in service because the mission and the cost are different.

items.headline: G-TEAD will award up to six OTAs after each Accelerated Capability Event
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 16 that the Army's Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate will award five to six other-transaction agreements after an Accelerated Capability Event, instead of one. Col. Christopher Hill, the director, told reporters Friday that the awards let small and medium-sized businesses that make it through a competition leave with an agreement, and that these agreements fund a 45-day operational assessment rather than a prototype. Breaking Defense said that assessment can then lead to one to three prototype agreements. The change started with an event in Hawaii, run with the Army's Pacific Command, on autonomous ground vehicles and command-and-control systems for sustainment and casualty evacuation, and Hill said the winners have not been named.

items.headline: Army moves PADDS users onto the Army Contract Writing System
items.summary: Army.mil reported Nov. 12, datelined Fort Belvoir, that the Army retired the Standard Procurement System earlier in fiscal 2026 and migrated users and contract actions from the Procurement Automated Data and Document System to the Army Contract Writing System. During the fiscal year-end surge the system migrated over 20,000 contract files in 90 days and trained over 1,100 users in the fourth quarter, and as of Oct. 1 more than 9,600 contracting professionals worldwide had access. Doug Haskin, project manager at Capability Program Executive Enterprise Software and Services, said the platform lets the Army respond more rapidly to emerging requirements. Lt. Col. Camille Morgan, product manager for the system, said migrating thousands of legacy files protected warfighter procurement needs while building an audit-ready enterprise, and final PADDS decommissioning continues through late 2026.

items.headline: 25th Infantry Division says it is pushing next-gen command-and-control compute to company level
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 12 that the 25th Infantry Division and partners are in Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center Rotation 27-01 in Hawaii, after the 11th Airborne Division flew 300 paratroopers 3,000 miles from Alaska. Maj. Gen. Jeff VanAntwerp, the division commander, said the 25th is one of two next-generation command-and-control-enabled divisions and that its cloud-based architecture pushes a good amount of compute from brigades down to the company level. He said the division is adding a secure network on top of mesh radios and commercially available devices so dispersed units have more computing power and tools for commanders. In the Lightning Surge 6 exercise, soldiers are limiting electronic transmissions at night and testing whether they can stay connected on tactical mesh radios and secure, unclassified data layers ahead of a long-range maritime air assault.

items.headline: Breaking Defense: a CNAS fellow says NGC2 has to connect nodes thousands of miles apart
items.summary: Breaking Defense reported Nov. 11 an interview with Josh Wallin, a defense program fellow at the Center for a New American Security, on the Army's Next Generation Command and Control effort. Wallin said an Indo-Pacific fight raises the problem of connecting systems that may be thousands of miles apart, and that bandwidth is strained by the volume of transmissions needed to keep distributed forces synchronized. He said NGC2 is trying to separate data links and radios from compute and from the data layer, so a jammed satellite terminal could be swapped without rebuilding the software above it. He also said the Army wants data that used to sit in separate air-defense, logistics, and fires systems to be usable across functions, with artificial intelligence used to automate parts of analysis that are still manual.
